'''''Eucalyptus grandis''''', commonly known as the '''flooded gum''' or '''rose gum''',<ref name="Boland" /> is a tall tree with smooth [[Bark (botany)|bark]], rough at the base fibrous or flaky, grey to grey-brown. At maturity, it reaches {{convert|50|m|ft|abbr=off}} tall, though the largest specimens can exceed {{convert|80|m|ft|abbr=off}} tall. It is found on coastal areas and sub-coastal ranges from [[Newcastle, New South Wales|Newcastle]] in New South Wales Australia northwards to west of [[Daintree, Queensland|Daintree]] in Queensland, mainly on flat land and lower slopes, where it is the dominant tree of wet forests and on the margins of rainforests.

[[File:Grandis Tree tallest in NSW.jpg|thumb|"The Grandis", a 400-year-old ''E. grandis'', the tallest tree in New South Wales, in [[Myall Lakes National Park]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Grandis picnic area – Myall Lakes National Park |url=https://www.nationalparks.nsw.gov.au/things-to-do/picnic-areas/grandis-picnic-area |website=nationalparks.nsw.gov.au |access-date=22 January 2025}}</ref>]]
[[File:EgrandisAlexFCA2.jpg|thumb|Lower trunk showing rough "skirt", [[Sunshine Coast, Queensland|Sunshine Coast]]]][[File:Eucalyptus grandis buds.jpg|thumb|Flower buds]]
[[File:Eucalyptus grandis fruit.jpg|thumb|Fruit]][[File:Eucalyptus grandis.jpg|thumb|right|Cultivated specimen in [[Maranoa Gardens]]]]

==Description==
''Eucalyptus grandis'' grows as a straight and tall forest tree, reaching around {{convert|50|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall,<ref name="floransw">{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Eucalyptus|species=grandis|author=Hill, Ken}}</ref> with a [[Diameter at breast height|dbh]] of {{convert|1.2|to|2|m|ft|abbr=on}}. The biggest trees can reach {{convert|75|m|ft|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|3|m|ft|abbr=on}} dbh,<ref name="Boland"/> the tallest recorded known as "The Grandis" near [[Bulahdelah]], with a height of {{convert|86|m|ft|abbr=on}} and a girth of {{convert|8.5|m|ft|abbr=on}}.<ref name=celebration>{{cite book|author1=Wrigley, John |author2=Fagg, Murray |title=Eucalypts: A Celebration|publisher=Allen & Unwin|year=2010|isbn=978-1-74175-924-2|pages=84, 157, 217}}</ref> The bole is straight for 2/3 to 3/4 the height of the tree. The bark is smooth and powdery, pale- or blue-grey to white in colour, with a skirt of rough brownish bark for the bottom {{cvt|1–4|m}} of the tree trunk.<ref name="Boland"/><!-- cites previous 3.5 sentences --> The glossy dark green [[leaf|leaves]] are stalked, [[lanceolate]] to broad lanceolate, and paler on their undersides, {{convert|10|to|16|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|–|3|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide. They are arranged alternately along the branches.<ref name="floransw"/> The secondary veins arise off the leaf midvein at a wide angle (61 degrees), and the leaf is dotted with around 800 oil glands per square centimetre.<ref>{{cite book|last=Brooker|first=Ian|author2=Nicolle, Dean|title=Atlas of Leaf Venation and Oil Gland Patterns in the Eucalypts|publisher=Csiro Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|date=2013|pages=57|isbn=9780643109865}}</ref>

The flower buds are arranged in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s in groups of seven, nine or eleven on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|10-18|mm}} long, the individual buds [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] or on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] up to {{cvt|5|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval, pear-shaped or club-shaped, green to yellow or [[wikt:glaucous#Adjective|glaucous]], {{cvt|6-9|mm}} long and {{cvt|4-5|mm}} wide. The white flowers appear from mid autumn to late winter from April to August. The flowers are followed by conical, pear- or cone-shaped fruit {{cvt|4-10|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-8|mm}} wide with the valves at rim level or slightly above.<ref name="floransw"/><ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus grandis'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_grandis.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=2 June 2020}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus grandis'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20grandis |publisher=Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=22 July 2019}}</ref>

The Sydney blue gum (''[[Eucalyptus saligna|E. saligna]]'') is very similar in appearance and overlaps ''E. grandis'' in the southern part of its range, but has narrower leaves and more bell-shaped gumnuts with protruding valves.<ref name=Hallstreet>{{cite book |title=A Field Guide to Australian Trees |last=Holliday |first=Ivan |year=1989 |publisher=Hamlyn Australia |location=Melbourne |isbn=0-947334-08-4 |page=198}}</ref> It also has a lignotuber. The mountain blue gum (''[[Eucalyptus deanei|E. deanei]]'') can be distinguished by its entirely smooth bark and wider adult leaves.<ref name="Boland"/>

==Taxonomy==
''Eucalyptus grandis'' was first formally described by [[Walter Hill (garden curator)|Walter Hill]] in 1862 in ''Catalogue of the Natural and Industrial Products of Queensland''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus grandis''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454690|publisher=APNI|access-date=22 July 2019}}</ref> The species name ''grandis'' "large" relates to this tree's large size. It is commonly known as the flooded gum and as rose gum in Queensland.<ref name="Boland">{{cite book|author1=Boland, Douglas J. |author2=Brooker, M. I. H. |author3=Chippendale, G. M. |author4=McDonald, Maurice William |title=Forest trees of Australia|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|location=Collingwood, Victoria|year=2006|page=292|isbn=0-643-06969-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CRQg11hSJ1kC&pg=PA84}}</ref><!-- cites previous 2 sentences --> It has been classified in the subgenus ''Symphyomyrtus'', Section ''Latoangulatae'', Series ''Transversae'' (eastern blue gums) by Brooker and Kleinig. Its two closest relatives are the Sydney blue gum (''[[Eucalyptus saligna]]'') and the mountain blue gum (''[[Eucalyptus deanei|E. deanei]]'').<ref name=brooker>{{cite book|title=Field Guide to Eucalypts|volume=1: South-eastern Australia|author1=Brooker, M.I.H. |author2=Kleinig, D. A. |pages=69–72 |publisher= Bloomings Books|location= Melbourne, Victoria |year= 1999|isbn=1-876473-03-7}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''E. grandis'' is found on coastal areas and sub-coastal ranges from the vicinity of [[Newcastle, New South Wales|Newcastle]] in [[New South Wales]] northwards to [[Bundaberg, Queensland|Bundaberg]] in central Queensland with disjunct populations further north near [[Mackay, Queensland|Mackay]], [[Townsville]] and [[Daintree, Queensland|Daintree]] in northern [[Queensland]], mainly on flat land and lower slopes. The soils are deep fertile [[alluvial]] loams. The annual rainfall varies from 1100 to 3500 mm.<ref name="Boland"/> It is the dominant tree of wet forest and rain forest margins,<ref name="floransw"/> either growing in pure stands or mixed with trees such as blackbutt (''[[Eucalyptus pilularis|E. pilularis]]''), tallowwood (''[[Eucalyptus microcorys|E. microcorys]]''), red mahogany (''[[Eucalyptus resinifera|E. resinifera]]''), Sydney blue gum (''E. saligna''), pink bloodwood (''[[Corymbia intermedia]]''), turpentine (''[[Syncarpia glomulifera]]''), brush box (''[[Lophostemon confertus]]'') and forest oak (''[[Allocasuarina torulosa]]'').<ref name="Boland"/>

''Eucalyptus grandis'' has been grown successfully in plantations in wetter areas of Sri Lanka, particularly in the [[Badulla District|Badulla]] and [[Nuwara Eliya District]]s. Many parameters of climate and soil are similar to eastern Australia, and it has grown well on plains as well as hills previously used for growing tea. Grown for its wood and ease of cultivation, it is the fastest growing eucalypt in the country.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Sivananthawerl, T. |author2=Mitlohner, R. |title=Silviculture in the Tropics|editor1=Sven G. Nter |editor2=Sven Günter |editor3=Michael Weber |editor4=Bernd Stimm |editor5=Reinhard Mosandl |publisher=Springer|year=2011|pages=465–70|chapter=''Eucalyptus grandis'' and other important ''Eucalyptus'' species|isbn=978-3-642-19985-1|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4Xw0ArgjQHsC&q=%22Eucalyptus+grandis%22&pg=PA470}}</ref>

Plantations have also been successful in Uruguay where lumber is being exported to the United States under the trade name "Red Grandis".<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cofusa.com.uy/redgrandis-applications.php|title = URUFOR}}</ref>

Extensive plantations also exist in South Africa and Brazil.<ref name=celebration/>

==Uses==
Flooded gum is an attractive, straight-trunked tree much in demand outside [[Australia]] for timber and pulp. Within Australia, plantations exist in northern New South Wales, where seedlings have put on {{convert|7|m|ft|abbr=off}} of growth in their first year.<ref name=Hallstreet/> The timber has a pinkish tinge and is used in joinery, flooring, boat building, panelling and plywood.<ref name=celebration/> It has a straight grain, moderate durability and strength, and is resistant to ''[[Lyctus (beetle)|Lyctus]]'' borers.<ref name="Boland"/> Hybrids with river red gum (''[[Eucalyptus camaldulensis]]'') are used to combat salinity.<ref name=celebration/> ''Eucalyptus grandis'' is a food plant of paropsine beetles of the family Chrysomelidae and [[Christmas beetle]]s, the latter often defoliating trees of Australia's east coast. Clones of ''Eucalyptus grandis'' have been selected and bred on the basis of unpalatability to the brown Christmas beetle (''[[Anoplognathus chloropyrus]]'') to minimise damage to plantations.<ref name=johns2004>{{cite journal |author1=Johns, Caitlin V. |author2=Stone, Christine |author3=Hughes, Lesley |year=2004|title= Feeding preferences of the Christmas beetle ''Anoplognathus chloropyrus'' (Coleoptera: Scarabaeidae) and four paropsine species (Coleoptera: Chrysomelidae) on selected ''Eucalyptus grandis'' clonal foliage |journal= Australian Forestry |volume= 67| issue= 3 |pages= 184–90 | doi=10.1080/00049158.2004.10674932 |s2cid=84280012 | url=http://svc043.wic023v.server-web.com/pdf/pdf-members/afj/AFJ%202004%20v67/AFJ%20September%202004%2067-3/AFJ67%283%29%20sep2004-Johns.pdf}}</ref>

Other insect pests include the steelblue sawfly (''[[Perga dorsalis]]'') and the leafblister sawfly (''[[Phylacteophaga froggatti]]''), both of which prefer young trees.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Stone|first=C.|date=1993|title=Insect pest problems of eucalypt plantations in Australia 2. New South Wales|journal=Australian Forestry|volume=56|issue=4|pages=363–69|doi=10.1080/00049158.1993.10674627}}</ref>

The tree is too large for most gardens, but makes an attractive tree for large parks and farms, and can be used in riverbank stabilisation.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Elliot | first1=Rodger W. | last2=Jones | first2=David L. | last3=Blake | first3=Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Vol. 4: Eu-Go |year=1992|pages=108–09 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-213-X}}</ref>

The saligna gum is grown extensively in plantations in South Africa in areas that formerly offered indifferent bee forage. At the onset of flowering each year an
extraordinarily large number of colonies move into these plantations where thousands are decoyed into hives by beekeepers. The flowers have a strong scent and beekeepers assert that bees travel at least 32 km (20 miles) to some plantations.
